newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia's Taylor favours strong leadership.
newsitem.headline: Liberia's Taylor favours strong leadership.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor, Liberia's president-elect, has always insisted that Africa's oldest republic needs a strong leader.
At 49, he has achieved through the ballotbox what he failed to achieve through the gun.
But critics say that the landslide vote in his favour in the July 19 elections to end the civil war he started has more to do with fear than love.

"Everyone is fully aware that Liberia needs a very strong leader," he told journalists at his heavily guarded home in Monrovia's Congotown suburb after his fighters and their rivals devastated the centre of the capital in April and May 1996.

"If Liberians are looking for a weak leader they are not going to find one in Charles Taylor," he said, rejecting suggestions he is a dictator in waiting. "I'm going to be a strong leader but I have also shown respect for others' views and values and I have also shown respect for law and order."
A former civil servant, whose child soldiers terrorised civilians with acts of mindless cruelty during the civil war, Taylor is charismatic and self-assured.
But he is a man who inspires mixed emotions.
"He deserves a bullet in the head," one foreign businessman once commented dryly of the man who plunged the West African nation into seven years of political and ethnic bloodshed.
His enthusiastic followers, many in their teens or 20s, say that as leader of the largest militia before disarmament this year he is the best guarantee of peace in Liberia.
Critics said if he lost he would make Liberia ungovernable.

"He killed my father but I'll vote for him," one voter told reporters during Saturday's landmark national elections. "He started all this and he's going to fix it," he said, summing up the dream of countless war-weary civilians.
The national elections commission pronounced Taylor president-elect of Liberia on Thursday with 75.3 percent of valid votes cast in the election.

"I think the Liberian people are saying to the world that we are ready for democracy...and that we must put violence behind us and look at the new millennium," Taylor said after voting. "There is no violence now and there will be no violence after."
Freed American slaves founded Liberia as Africa's first independent republic in 1847 with a constitution based on that of the United States.
Taylor, a teetotal, U.S.-educated Baptist, describes himself as a friend of the United States and an admirer of former presidents Richard Nixon and Ronald Reagan.

He enjoyed a distinct campaign advantage over his 11 rivals with a well-oiled electoral machine backed by his own national radio station. His rallies, free T-shirts and other giveaways drew enthusiastic crowds, many of them teenagers.
Born on January 29, 1948, Taylor had a native Liberian mother and a father of the mixed Americo-Liberian stock.
He marched into his West African homeland from Ivory Coast on Christmas Eve 1989 with a band of 150 associates reputed to be Libyan-trained. Taylor denies any Libyan links.
His plan was to oust Master Sergeant Samuel Doe, who broke the hold on power of the descendants of the freed slaves.
His National Patriotic Front of Liberia forces, a mix of descendants of slaves and indigenous tribes such as Mano and Gio, twice fought to the edge of the capital Monrovia.
Twice, a Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force, ECOMOG, thwarted them -- fuelling animosity between Taylor and regional giant Nigeria that helped perpetuate the conflict.
After well over 150,000 deaths and the bloody 1996 flare-up in Monrovia, Liberia's neighbours finally rallied its squabbling warlords around a peace deal that held.
ECOMOG, long denounced by Taylor as an occupation army, ensured peace and disarmament, making the elections possible.
During most of the war, Taylor was based in his northern stronghold of Gbarnga. He finally entered Monrovia in 1995, after signing a power-sharing agreement with his rivals.

Taylor and Nigeria had buried the hatchet, with Taylor travelling to its capital Abuja to sign the peace deal. The deal collapsed but much of the animosity that poisoned relations between the two was laid to rest.
Taylor was widely blamed for the breakdown of a dozen or so deals to end the war, which smashed the economy and forced over half the pre-war population of 2.5 million from their homes.
Many Liberians hold him responsible for triggering the 1996 showdown with indigenous Krahn in Monrovia. Widespread looting devastated the capital, until then largely spared by fighting.
In the runup to elections, Taylor made a barely disguised threat to the election commissioner after rivals sought a poll delay.

"If Henry Andrews attempts to postpone these elections, only the angels, not even ECOMOG will protect him," Taylor told state radio on July 8. "If he does I am going to provide him with money for his plane ticket to leave the country."
An economics graduate educated at Bentley College outside Boston, Taylor was active in a U.S.-based student movement critical of William Tolbert, toppled and killed by Doe in 1980.
He fled Liberia in 1983, accused of embezzlement by Doe's government, which sought his extradition from the United States. Taylor escaped from a U.S. jail using a hacksaw and bedsheets.
Taylor is married with eight children.
